newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan pension fund says to take more risks.
newsitem.headline: Japan pension fund says to take more risks.

text.p: After receiving a long-awaited green light for freer management, a key Japanese pension fund is ready to take on more risks and has decided to beef up its stock investments, a top official with the fund says.

Japan's Pension Fund Association will increase its share of investment for both overseas and domestic stocks from October, while cutting down that of fixed-income assets, said Yasunobu Takayama, general manager of its investment department.
"We will put more emphasis on stocks, both domestic and foreign," Takayama told Reuters in an interview.
The association, which oversees the country's numerous corporate pension funds, is itself a fund managing a total of almost three trillion yen ($27.0 billion).
It serves as a pension fund for workers who have left corporations before being eligible for pension payments.
Takayama said that from October, roughly half of the fund's portfolio will be divided equally between equities and bonds.

Previously, the fund had to abide by the so-called "5-3-3-2" rule, which stipulated that its portfolio consist of 50 percent fixed-income instruments, 30 percent each for domestic stocks and foreign currency-denominated assets, and the remaining 20 percent for real estate investment.

Following the government's deregulatory measures announced in spring, the fund was given permission for freer management in July and has decided to take action from October, when the second half of the Japanese fiscal year begins, Takayama said.
"We drew up a portfolio which allows us to take more risks," he said.
In the new portfolio, the share of fixed-income instruments, mainly domestic bonds, will be lowered to 38 percent from nearly 50 percent in the current portfolio.
In contrast, the share of domestic stocks will be raised to 30 percent from around 20 percent, and that of foreign stocks to 14 percent from the current 10 percent.
Little change was made in foreign bond investment, which retained a share of approximately six percent.
Along with the change in its portfolio, the fund will also entrust more of its assets to investment advisory firms at the expense of life insurers and trust banks, Takayama said.
Excluding the 120 billion yen ($1.08 billion) that the fund will manage on its own, most of its total assets of 2.8 trillion yen ($25.2 billion) will be entrusted to financial institutions, he added.

Funds entrusted to life insurers, currently amounting to approximately 350 billion yen ($3.15 billion), will be slashed by half, while the 1.57 trillion yen ($14.1 billion) allocated to trust banks will be cut by 100 billion yen ($900 million), Takayama said.

He said many Japanese trust banks' performances in investing in foreign stocks was poor, added that a large part of the new funds will be entrusted to foreign advisory firms for the management of foreign stocks.
The decision to cut back on the assets managed by life insurers follows the insurers' move in April to lower their guaranteed returns to 2.5 percent from 4.5 percent, he added.

Takayama said the pension fund aims for an overall return of around six percent for the new portfolio, taking into account the 5.5 percent return it guarantees to pensioners and costs such as advisory fees paid to financial institutions.
The association officially explained its new portfolio to the institutions to which it entrusts its funds and made the allocation changes last Wednesday, Takayama said.
He added that the fund plans to stick to the new portfolio for at least three years before a revision. ($1=111 yen)
